title: The Satipatthana (Mindfulness) Sutra
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The teacher invites listeners to explore the Satipatthana Sutta, a foundational Buddhist teaching on mindfulness, by cultivating awareness of the present moment without attachment or aversion. This practice is meant to lead to greater self-understanding and wisdom, allowing individuals to see things as they truly are, rather than being clouded by preconceptions or biases. By embracing this approach, one can begin to shed illusions that hinder spiritual growth and move closer to embodying the Buddha's teachings in their own lives.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning all.
It's interesting, I just realized as I was chanting that we always say "the truth of the Tathagata's words."
The Dharma talk might include current events, all kinds of new books, psychology, and so on.
But today it's actually going to be about the Tathagata's words.
It's the words of the Pali Canon, the oldest Buddhist writings.
There are several collections, and they are not ordered much by subject, but by the length of the talks.
So we have the Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha, and that's what I'm going to talk about today.
It's in this lovely skinny book here.
The Middle Length Discourses are 150 discourses.
We could almost say they were the Dharma talks of the Tathagata.
Maybe they were delivered in a series, because some of them are definitely too long to be delivered on the spot in one go.
And then there are also the Long Discourses of the Buddha.
I fell in love with these writings on two separate occasions.
One was when I was proofreading for Project Gutenberg, and I ran across the Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha in German.
They were translated by Carl Eugen Neumann, an Austrian.
I understand nowadays that his translation was maybe not 100 percent accurate.
There have been some criticisms of him using specific words and so on.
They talked about the Buddha in a different way, and I could see a love shining through that I have not seen in other translations.
It's been my firm understanding, not scientifically based, but I was wondering what can motivate one to wander through the Indian plains and mountains for so many years, teaching the Dharma.
Maybe awakening will do it.
But in my understanding, it was love.
The Buddha doesn't talk about love, not in words, but his actions combined with what he taught.
This is how I understand it.
If anybody thinks it should get corrected, let's talk.
So today I want to talk about one of the 150 discourses from the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle Length Discourses.
It's actually quite a famous one.
The second time I fell in love with those writings was when I was training to become a mindfulness teacher, which I am now, but I'm not practicing it.
All of the mindfulness teachings come from one of the fascicles in the Majjhima Nikaya, one of the 150 fascicles.
This is the binder from my first year of training, all the information we were handed and so on.
All of that is based on the Satipatthana Sutta, the foundations of mindfulness.
In this book, it represents 11 pages.
And it's become the mindfulness movement that has been going on for the last, I don't know exactly how long.
Probably about 40 years ago, it started on a small scale.
I'm going to officially start today's Dharma talk, after this introduction, with the reading of the introduction of the mindfulness sutra, the foundations of mindfulness.
*Thus have I heard.
On one occasion, the Blessed One was living in the Kuru country, where there was a town of the Kurus named Kamasadamma.
There he addressed the Bhikkhus thus: "Bhikkhus."
"Venerable sir," they replied.

The Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, this is the direct path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, for the realization of nirvana, namely the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?*
*Here, Bhikkhus, a Bhikkhu abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
He abides contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief of the world.
He abides contemplating mind as mind, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
He abides contemplating mind objects as mind objects, ardent, fully aware and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world."*
I'd like to explain some words.
The opening of the sutra is "Thus have I heard," and that is a standard opening for all sutras.
In the early collections, it means that Ananda is speaking.
He was the Buddha's attendant, and fortunately, he had an eidetic memory and could basically memorize all the talks that the Buddha gave.
So the "I" in "Thus have I heard" is Ananda.
The word Bhikkhus means monks.
For our context today, he is addressing all of us, whether we are lay, whether we are ordained, whether we are living in a monastery or whether we live as householders.
The four foundations of mindfulness are body as a body, feelings as feelings, mind as mind, mind objects as mind objects.
Often, instead of mind objects, we say phenomena when we talk about these teachings.
So basically anything we can see, touch, those are the phenomena.
The other thing that I just want to mention very briefly is that when they talk about feelings in these discourses, they usually do not talk about emotions.
It's not about am I feeling happy or sad, but it is on a level underneath, a lower level.
Basically, the Buddha is asking us to watch our likes and dislikes.
Let me dig one more level deeper.
It doesn't mean that we don't think pleasant and unpleasant or neutral, because those are just true experiences.
Whenever we encounter something, there is either this feeling of pleasant, unpleasant or neutral.
When we walk out of a cold house into the warm sunshine, our whole body says pleasant.
If we trip and fall and break our nose, our body says unpleasant.
And if we pretty much don't know anything or we don't have any special relationship to something, it's neutral.
For me, I use the color blue.
I see blue.
I don't particularly have any reaction to it.
So it's very, very basic.
We should not stop finding things pleasant or unpleasant.
The Buddha is not asking that of us.
He is asking that we do not insert ourselves into the pleasant and unpleasant.
My question is, what happens when pleasant, unpleasant gets mixed up with ego?
Then it becomes liking and disliking, which is something really different.
It would be, "Oh, I dislike the color pink.
"I never like pink.
I will not ever like pink.
I will not wear pink clothing."
That is when I insert myself into that chain.
When I fall and I break my nose, I definitely go unpleasant.
But as soon as I say, "Oh, I really don't like that I broke my nose, what the hell am I going to look like from now on?
And I trip, blood on my clothing, I really hate that," and so on, that's the ego.
So let's keep the ego out of it.
Now, let me capture this.
Those are the two places in my life where I really fell in love with the Pali Canon.
Once with the writings of Carl Eugen Neumann, which really opened another world of Buddhist understanding for me, and the mindfulness training, which really explores the Satipatthana Sutta.
It's so interesting that something else we've been practicing recently is strongly going to come into the picture, which is the teachings of Thich Nhat Hanh.
One of the nicknames that he's been given is Mr.
Mindfulness.
Someone once told me that just seeing him walking down a path in that incredible way that he was walking changed his life.
Just seeing Thich Nhat Hanh walking and moving had a great impact on many people.
So the big question is around mindfulness.
Can we look more deeply and clearly at what we are doing?
Can we do it in a way that is more thoughtful and more inclusive and therefore more interesting in the end?
Do you find that when you practice meditation, and when meditation is a part of your way of accessing your experience, it gives you a different point of view?
Joseph Goldstein, who was one of the originators of today's mindfulness movement, has a definition of mindfulness.
He said mindfulness is awareness that arises through paying attention on purpose in the present moment, non-judgmentally, in the service of self-understanding and wisdom.
Let me read that one more time.
Mindfulness is awareness that arises through paying attention on purpose in the present moment, non-judgmentally, in the service of self-understanding and wisdom.
Now I will speak a bit more about the secular mindfulness movement.
Around 1976, Joseph Goldstein, Jack Kornfield, and Sharon Salzberg founded the Insight Meditation Center in Barre, Massachusetts.

They all had studied Buddhism in South Asia, and their goal was to create a meditation center that would remain in the American context, but to teach what they had experienced and learned in Southeast Asia.
Apparently, there was a deliberate intention on the teacher side to not promote the Buddhist elements of chanting and ceremony and magic and miracles that they had practiced in Southeast Asia.
Their center was focused on meditation and mindfulness.
They also included Western elements, such as psychology and psychotherapy.
And now we circle back to our practice period that just finished.
The second main factor in this movement was Thich Nhat Hanh.
He was a Vietnamese Buddhist monk, and his students fondly called him Thay, teacher.
He was exiled from his country at one point, and he became known in the US as a speaker and a peace activist who was working hard to bring an end to the Vietnam War in the 1960s.
In the 1970s, he shifted his focus to promote mindfulness and meditation.
One of his most well-known books is called The Miracle of Mindfulness.
One tragedy was that he was suspect to both governments, one in Vietnam and one in the US.
Suspected to be a capitalist by one country and suspected to be a communist by the other.
I founded Plum Village in France, and now more than 350 official meditation practice groups are affiliated with Thich Nhat Hanh's teachings worldwide.
I actually think that number 350 is not correct.
I trust there are more of them, but I don't know.
Along with the Dalai Lama, he was one of the most revered and best known Buddhist teachers.
Thich Nhat Hanh passed away last year in 2022 at the age of 94.
He had experienced a stroke some years before and lived out the end of his life in his home temple in Vietnam.
It's incredible how much this mindfulness movement took hold of the US.
We often talk about Buddhism taking on the characteristics of the country it is practiced in.
In the US, of course, it did become a commercial movement and not so much a spiritual movement.
Now I'm going to insert my opinion.
Please note this is just my opinion.
I wondered why that was so.
Why are our sanghas, our Buddhist sanghas, inviting everybody in and teaching, everybody can listen to Dharma talks without any financial exchange,
while the mindfulness movement is mostly commercial?
You sign up for an eight-week mindfulness practice, mindfulness teaching, and you pay your fee and then you go on.
That is an interesting question.
One of the reasons, I think, is that the mindfulness teaching is utterly secular.
It's not said, but it's in a way a bit of a self-improvement program, even though originally secular mindfulness was used in the health care sector.
I am quoting Jon Kabat-Zinn, who said hospitals and medical centers in this society are dukkha magnets.
He used the Pali word for suffering.
People are drawn to hospitals primarily when they are suffering.
So it's very natural to introduce programs to help them deal with the enormity of their suffering in a systematic way, as a complement to medical efforts.

To be accepted in secular society, at least officially secular society as the U.S., Jon Kabat-Zinn realized that he needed to change his approach and remove any religious connections from his teaching.

So he reframed the foundations of mindfulness as a mental skill that can be acquired through meditation. [unclear: "of his mindfulness movement"], paying attention in a particular way on purpose in the present moment, non-judgmentally, in the service of self-knowledge and wisdom.
That "in the service of self-knowledge and wisdom" often does not appear in the definitions, but I think it's essential to include it.
By promoting mindfulness and teaching meditations, patients in hospitals were taught how to manage the dukkha associated with their physical condition.
The training enabled them to be more accepting of their life, their body, their experience, which would then in turn lessen pain, anxiety and depression.
Of course, that doesn't say anything about the need for medical treatment.
I mean, we don't say be mindful the cancer away or something like that.

But the mindfulness movement was originally created to help speed the recovery process by having a more positive attitude going through it, and preparing patients to successfully navigate future experiences and decisions.
So which Buddhist teaching does this remind us of?
Accepting experience and not going into pain, anxiety and depression over it.
It goes back to the Buddha's teaching of the two darts.
The story of the two darts says this, in brief: sometimes we just get hit by a dart.
There is nothing we can do about it.
It came from behind.
I didn't see the person.
I didn't see the dart, and bang, I have this dart lodged in my upper arm.
Except for the "dang," this is all facts.
I was being really bad by saying things, because that inserts myself into the story.
But here I'm sitting with that dart, and the second dart in the story of the two darts is coming from me, by fretting and being anxious and unhappy and angry that this happened to me.
I could just go ahead and pull out the dart, put on a bandaid and go on my merry way.
But instead I'm sitting here and I'm wondering if the dart was poisoned.
The clothing that was ruined, damn, I just bought the shirt and now it's ruined.
I was planning on going swimming this afternoon and now I can't, because I have this leaking hole in my body, and so on.
Trying to figure out who was it that hit me with the dart and how can I get back to that person?
I want revenge.
I want to make them suffer like I did.
So the first one is just the facts.
We can just say, okay, I'll pull out the dart, wash it out, put a bandaid on it and act in an appropriate way.
The other one is the mind and the ego spinning out and getting obsessed with the second dart.
So when we're in the hospital, or if a loved one is in the hospital, my partner just had a stroke a couple of weeks ago, and he had to go to the emergency room and hospital and so on.
And I, of course, you know, is he going to come back?
Will he be well?
Can we manage this with our resources and so on?
Yeah, it's kind of natural that it comes up.
But when we notice the mind trip we are going on, we can impact that.
We can mindfully consider the facts and have our life.
There is a little bit more I would like to tell you before I'm going to close the talk.
Mindfulness, sati in Pali, is from the earliest Buddhist teachings.
The foundations of mindfulness are also called the discourse on the establishing of mindfulness.
If you would like to look it up, there is a copy on the Access to Insight website.
If you just Google it, you will find it under the discourses of the Buddha.
Like I said, it's short.
It's 11 pages long.
And it's incredible how much that has been processed and applied to different physical and mental conditions and how helpful it has been to people in general.
As far as we know, the Buddha's definition of sati was pretty straightforward: keeping something in mind, that is, continuously remembering the object you're aiming to keep your attention on.
So when a Buddhist teacher talks about mindfulness of the breath, they're talking about remembering the breath and maintaining awareness of the breath.
Other meanings the Buddha connected with mindfulness in his discourse were being alert, being ardent, being intent,
and experiencing with comprehension of what is and what is going on.
So it's not just a stripped-down attention.
It's not just breath in, breath out and so on.

One last thing I would like to say about the mindfulness movement, which I had mentioned in the beginning, is that the teaching in the mindfulness courses does not include any ethical or moral admonitions such as the precepts, such as the Brahma Viharas, or nothing that reminds of religious teachings.
Thank you very much for your attention and listening to this talk.
If you think it was helpful, please practice what the Buddha taught.
And if you do not find it helpful, please forget every word said in the last half hour.
Thank you so very much.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.*
*Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
